initial_requirements: Military services need a common Tactical Control System for operating different current and future unmanned aerial vehicles and their payloads. Operators should be able to plan and control missions, monitor aircraft and payload status, receive and process sensor information, and distribute imagery and other mission products. The system must also exchange tasking and operational information with the wider command-and-control environment.

slots.value: Step in when there’s a safety issue, an unexpected change in the mission, a communications problem, or anything that pushes the aircraft outside the planned envelope. They can approve a high-risk action, override a planned task, or take control if the operator can’t continue safely or the mission needs to be redirected quickly. Their authority is to protect the mission and the aircraft, and keep the operation aligned with command intent. Main triggers include loss of positive control, degraded link quality, unexpected airspace conflict, sensor or payload behavior affecting safety, requests to deviate from the approved mission profile, crossing a preapproved boundary such as altitude, route, or payload-use restriction, and changes in rules of engagement or tasking. In those cases, the supervisor can pause, approve the exception, or take over control until the situation is stable.

slots.key: Mission ownership and queued tasking visibility
slots.value: The active mission should stay owned by the current controlling station or unit. A new tasking should remain separate from the live mission if it is just informational or still under review. If it is compatible with the current route, payload, timing, and authority, it can be linked or merged so the operator can apply it without rebuilding the mission from scratch. If it is related but not yet approved, it should be shown alongside the live mission as a candidate change so the controller can compare them without risk of accidentally executing it.

topics.topic_content: Mission execution phases and operator actions during flight

slots.key: Launch, en-route, on-station, and recovery phases
slots.value: Support launch-to-recovery operations across the full mission, with aircraft status visible throughout; response must occur within the window where the aircraft is still safe and the mission can still be recovered, making speed operationally relevant rather than tied to a fixed number today. Urgency varies a lot by mission phase and decision type: in launch, recovery, or any degraded state the response needs to be essentially immediate because the aircraft may not tolerate delay; during steady-state cruise or routine sensing there is usually a little more time. If the aircraft is still controllable, options are being preserved, but once it is already in recovery the window tightens and the system should prioritize the fastest safe action or escalation. During launch and recovery the interface should emphasize aircraft health, link quality, and immediate safety cues; en route it should lean toward route, fuel or endurance, and task progress; during target or collection activity it should put the payload view and mission objective front and center; in degraded operation it should shift hard toward fault status, lost-link handling, and quick recovery decision support.

slots.value: Current mission plan should not be overwritten without review; preserve the active plan and present new tasking as a change or re-tasking request so the operator can assess whether it can be merged, queued, or whether the aircraft needs to transition to a new profile. slots.key: Aborts, contingencies, and mission suspend behavior
slots.value: A supervisor or mission commander may step in when there is a safety issue, an unexpected change in the mission, a communications problem, or anything that pushes the aircraft outside the planned envelope. They can approve a high-risk action, override a planned task, or take control if the operator cannot continue safely or the mission needs to be redirected quickly. Their authority is to pause the mission, override a specific operator action, reassign tasks, take full control when needed, and hand control back to the operator once the situation is resolved and the transfer is acknowledged; the most critical cases are safety interventions, control handoffs, target or sensor retasking, and anything affecting airspace deconfliction or mission authorization because wrong or delayed action there can have immediate consequences. When phases overlap or change suddenly, the system should automatically elevate aircraft control and recovery-type actions ahead of planning, payload work, or product distribution whenever there is any conflict; the current task gets suspended or downgraded until the higher-priority control need is satisfied, unless an authorized exception is specifically declared.

topics.topic_content: Core vehicle control functions for unmanned aircraft operation

slots.value: Control missions; platform variation should be hidden as much as possible, but only platform-supported mission types, control modes, and sensor commands should be exposed, and unsupported actions must be blocked. Reuse the common interface as-is when the new UAV behaves the same way from the operator’s point of view for planning, control, payload management, and mission reporting. Any difference that changes safety, airspace compliance, mission authority, or payload employment requires a program-specific control rule or restriction, including unique launch and recovery limits, special lost-link behavior, different sensor slew or collection constraints, and weapons or sensitive payload handling rules. If the UAV cannot truly follow the same operator action without a different risk profile, it should not be treated as fully common.

slots.key: Manual versus supervised autonomy control split
slots.value: A supervisor or mission commander may pause the mission, override a specific operator action, reassign tasks, and take full control when needed; local pause or override is appropriate for contained issues such as a bad sensor action or an unexpected route change, while full control is used for safety, communications loss, or a major mission deviation. They can hand control back to the operator once the situation is resolved and the transfer is acknowledged. Response needs to occur within the window where the aircraft is still safe and the mission can still be recovered, so it is about operational relevance rather than a fixed number. Accurate control actions require the operator or commander to have the right aircraft state, payload state, and mission context to act without guessing. topics.topic_content: Exception conditions and degraded control behavior

slots.key: Degraded command links and fallback control mode
slots.value: Account for limited or contested communications and intermittent bandwidth; keep the system usable when links degrade so operators can still monitor status, queue actions, and recover a mission even if they cannot do everything in real time. In degraded communications, the real-time essentials are basic aircraft status, link status, location, fuel or endurance, major faults, and payload state if it affects flight or safety; detailed health trends, full sensor housekeeping, and non-urgent mission logs can be queued for later. Lost-link recovery remains a special case. In degraded communications or lost-link recovery, the handling has to be more protective, with automatic safing and only limited changes allowed until control is re-established. During degraded communications, the operator should be able to command a safe fallback, redirect the aircraft if link still permits, or approve recovery actions, while the system automatically handles low-level stability and timeout behavior. If the link is fully lost, the system should follow preapproved lost-link logic without waiting for operator input. Mission continuation, pausing, or termination should depend on mission rules, airspace constraints, and payload; if recovery cannot be done safely or the aircraft is outside approved limits, it should terminate or return rather than keep pressing on.

slots.value: Behavior must account for different sensor loads, varying levels of automation, and whether control is local crew, remote crew, or passed between control elements; it must also represent station state clearly as local, remote, primary, or backup, and support intermittent links and delayed updates during handoff or control transfer. slots.value: Supervisor should be able to pause the mission, override a specific operator action, reassign tasks, take full control when needed, and hand control back to the operator once the situation is resolved and the transfer is acknowledged. A pause or local override is appropriate for contained issues like a bad sensor action or an unexpected route change; full control is for safety, communications loss, or a major mission deviation. If the aircraft is still controllable, the system should preserve options; once it is already in recovery, the window tightens and the system should prioritize the fastest safe action or escalation. If a mission is already in progress, do not force the cutover mid-flight unless there is a very clear operational need and a validated handoff procedure; otherwise wait until the aircraft is back in a stable state. If the lag is severe enough to affect safety, the operator should be prevented from making time-sensitive decisions off that display until it recovers.

slots.key: Preplanned surveillance authority and change control
slots.value: The system should stay conservative and keep the approved route and payload setup unless an operator explicitly authorizes a change. Any change that affects where the aircraft goes, what the sensor is looking at, when it collects, or how it behaves should require explicit operator authorization before execution. Small background updates like display-only status changes or non-operative metadata should not require that level of approval. If the change could alter collection, safety, or coordination with other forces, the system should stop and ask for clear human confirmation first.

slots.key: Timing thresholds and platform-specific edge cases
slots.value: Operator commands for route, payload state, or recovery behavior should be allowed only once the aircraft is in a stable state for that transition. The system must enforce correct sequencing for the specific platform. Route changes must not interrupt launch, recovery, or a critical payload action. Payload state changes must be blocked if the aircraft is outside the approved conditions for that payload. Recovery behavior is especially sensitive and may only be commanded when platform-specific boundaries are respected and the aircraft is in a state where the new behavior can take over safely.

Recovery behavior is especially sensitive and may only be commanded when platform-specific boundaries are respected and the aircraft is in a state where the new behavior can take over safely.

slots.key: Display latency handling and degraded indication
slots.value: There is no universal latency tolerance; acceptable latency depends on mission phase, platform type, the type of information displayed, and the mission’s safety and time sensitivity, with safety-critical phases using the strictest behavior. If the data is only slightly behind but still operationally useful, a delayed label may be enough; if it could mislead judgment, the system should switch to a degraded presentation; and if the lag could create a safety risk or mislead a time-sensitive action, it should block use for that purpose and force the operator to rely on current status or a different source. Thresholds should also consider the source’s declared freshness and confidence, because different sensors and external feeds age differently.

slots.key: Response timing relative to operational relevance
slots.value: Response timing varies by mission phase and decision type: in launch, recovery, or any degraded state it needs to be essentially immediate because the aircraft may not tolerate delay; during steady-state cruise or routine sensing there is usually a little more time. slots.key: Sensor display latency tolerance and fallback behavior
slots.value: Acceptable latency depends on the mission’s safety and time sensitivity, not just the source or update rate. If information is slower but still operationally useful, the system may label it as delayed; if it could mislead judgment, it should switch to a degraded presentation; and if using it could create a safety risk in that phase, it should be blocked for time-sensitive use. The system should also consider the source’s declared freshness and confidence, since different sensors and external feeds age differently.

revisions.new_value: Acceptable latency depends on the platform and mission phase rather than a universal number; the system should visibly indicate when the display is behind the feed, warn the operator or switch to a degraded indication if the delay crosses an operational threshold, and prevent time-sensitive decisions from being made off the display if the lag becomes severe enough to affect safety until it recovers.

revisions.old_value: Acceptable latency depends on the platform and mission phase rather than a universal number; the system should visibly indicate when the display is behind the feed, warn the operator or switch to a degraded indication if the delay crosses an operational threshold, and prevent time-sensitive decisions from being made off the display if the lag becomes severe enough to affect safety until it recovers.
revisions.new_value: Acceptable latency depends on the platform type, mission phase, and the type of information being displayed, with safety-critical phases using the strictest behavior. If the data is only slightly behind, the system may just label it as delayed; if it is materially stale, it should switch to a degraded view; and if the lag could mislead a time-sensitive action, it should block use for that purpose and force the operator to rely on current status or a different source. Thresholds should be configurable by program or mission profile because what is acceptable on one vehicle or phase may be unacceptable on another.

slots.value: Hand-off between operators or control stations needs to be very clean during preplanned surveillance, time-sensitive retask, degraded communications, lost-link recovery, and while payload tasking changes in flight; especially important for safety interventions, control handoffs, target or sensor retasking, and anything affecting airspace deconfliction or mission authorization because wrong or delayed action can have immediate consequences. The controlling station may change, and authority needs to move cleanly with the aircraft so there’s no ambiguity about who can command it. Allowed actions may differ by setup, with some stations only monitoring while others can fully command, including coalition operations and reach-back support. Current mission plans should not be overwritten without review; new tasking should be preserved as a change or re-tasking request for operator assessment, with possible merge, queue, or transition to a new profile. If the new tasking requires a different payload setup or control source, the handoff must be explicit so the system does not lose track of what is flying, who owns it, or which mission objective is current. Precedence should follow the current mission phase and the role with the highest immediate safety or operational impact, and any switch should require either a system-confirmed handoff or an approved role change so the person is not acting in two conflicting roles at once without the system knowing.

slots.value: When a re-tasking request arrives, route it through operator review first with enough context to judge whether it conflicts with the active mission, current authority, or flight and payload constraints. If the request is just informational or still under review, keep it separate from the live mission. If it is compatible with the current route, payload, timing, and authority, it can be linked or merged so the operator can apply it without rebuilding the mission from scratch. If it is related but not yet approved, show it alongside the live mission as a candidate change so the controller can compare them without any risk of accidentally executing it. If the retask fits within the current authority and doesn’t conflict with a critical phase of flight or collection, accept it quickly and immediately assess what it would displace. If the displacement is significant or could create a safety or mission conflict, hold it for review rather than auto-applying.

slots.key: Controlled release auditing and metadata marking
slots.value: Sharing and handoff should support controlled release, auditing, and metadata marking; when raw sensor data is released, it should be governed by classification, releasability, mission authority, and recipient approval for that specific data set. If any of those checks fail, the raw data should not be released at all. When released, sensitive collection details and operator identity should be stripped, only the minimum technical metadata needed to interpret the data should be retained, and the data should be marked with proper caveats, origin, time, and handling instructions so the context remains clear but controlled. The system should also log who touched the data, when, and what changed to preserve traceability in the wider command-and-control environment.

slots.value: Require an explicit acknowledgment from the external command-and-control side; receipt alone is not enough. topics.topic_content: Rules that govern what operators may do with missions, aircraft, and payloads

slots.key: Authority levels for mission control actions
slots.value: A station may be monitor-only when it lacks current authority, when the communications link is too limited for safe command, or when policy restricts it due to mission sensitivity, certification, or airspace constraints. It may command the aircraft when it has assigned control authority, the communications path is good enough, and the operator is cleared for that mission segment. The role can change during the mission, especially during handoff between sites or if the primary station loses connectivity and a backup takes over. When a person must cover multiple mission roles, precedence should follow the current mission phase and the role with the highest immediate safety or operational impact.

revisions.new_value: The system should hide platform variation as much as possible, but operators may only see and do what the specific UAV platform can actually support; unsupported mission types, control modes, and sensor commands must be blocked, and some platform-specific functions may require additional clearance or tighter control depending on mission and aircraft configuration.

revisions.old_value: The system should hide platform variation as much as possible, but operators may only see and do what the specific UAV platform can actually support; unsupported mission types, control modes, and sensor commands must be blocked, and some platform-specific functions may require additional clearance or tighter control depending on mission and aircraft configuration.

slots.key: Rules of engagement or mission authorization limits
slots.value: Mission execution must stop for supervisor or commander approval if there is a change in rules of engagement or tasking, or if the mission needs to cross a preapproved boundary such as an altitude, route, or payload-use restriction.

revisions.new_value: Mission execution must stop for supervisor or commander approval if there is a change in rules of engagement or tasking, or if the mission needs to cross a preapproved boundary such as an altitude, route, or payload-use restriction.

slots.value: Preplanned surveillance should remain on the approved route and payload setup unless an operator explicitly authorizes a change. Any change that affects where the aircraft goes, what the sensor is looking at, when it collects, or how it behaves should require explicit operator authorization before execution. Small background updates, like display-only status changes or non-operative metadata, shouldn’t need that level of approval. If the change could alter collection, safety, or coordination with other forces, the system should stop and ask for a clear human confirmation first. In addition, route changes should not interrupt launch, recovery, or a critical payload action, and payload state changes should be blocked unless the aircraft is in the approved conditions for that payload.

slots.key: Supervisor or mission commander intervention conditions and authority
slots.value: If a request is compatible with the current authority and doesn’t conflict with a critical phase of flight or collection, it can be accepted quickly and immediately assessed for what it would displace. The operator should see the impact on timing, route, payload use, and any already approved tasking before anything is executed. If the displacement is significant or could create a safety or mission conflict, it should hold for review rather than auto-applying.

revisions.new_value: A supervisor or mission commander steps in when there is a safety issue, an unexpected mission change, a communications problem, or any condition that pushes the aircraft outside the planned envelope. In those cases, they may approve a high-risk action, override a planned task, or take control if the operator cannot continue safely or the mission must be redirected quickly. Their authority is to protect the mission and aircraft and keep the operation aligned with command intent.

slots.value: The mission commander may pause the mission, override a specific operator action, reassign tasks, take full control when needed for safety, communications loss, or a major mission deviation, and hand control back to the operator once the situation is resolved and the transfer is acknowledged. Any switch between planning, aircraft control, payload operation, or product distribution should require either a system-confirmed handoff or an approved role change so the person is not acting in two conflicting roles at once without the system knowing. If handoff stays pending because external acknowledgment does not arrive, the system should show a clear pending-handoff status with the reason, the elapsed wait time, and what mission elements are still not authoritative. After a defined timeout, it should escalate to the operator and possibly a supervisor or alternate channel. It should not auto-complete the tasking unless explicitly approved by policy, and the previous confirmed tasking should remain active until the new acknowledgment arrives or an authorized contingency is invoked.

slots.key: Common interface reuse conditions for new UAVs
slots.value: A common interface can be reused as-is only when the new UAV truly behaves the same from the operator’s point of view. Any difference that changes safety, airspace compliance, mission authority, or payload employment requires a program-specific control rule or restriction. That includes unique launch and recovery limits, special lost-link behavior, different sensor slew or collection constraints, and any weapons or sensitive payload handling rules. If the UAV cannot follow the same operator action without a different risk profile, it should not be treated as fully common. Recovery behavior is especially sensitive and any command that alters it must respect platform-specific boundaries and only be allowed when the aircraft is in a state where the new behavior can take over safely.

revisions.new_value: A common interface can be reused as-is when the new UAV behaves the same way from the operator’s point of view for planning, control, payload management, and mission reporting. A program-specific variant is needed when there are meaningful differences in workflows, sensor controls, alerting, or safety constraints. Separate training is warranted when the differences are large enough that the same muscle memory or procedures would create confusion or increase risk.

slots.value: Mission planning and operator authority are bounded by mission assignment, platform status, command or rules-of-engagement constraints, airspace constraints, safety interlocks, and any higher-authorization requirements. Permitted actions include planning, launch, retasking within approved limits, and payload management. Changes are allowed only under clearly defined exceptions such as emergency recovery, safety-of-flight protection, or formally delegated higher authority. The system should require all mission-critical inputs before it accepts an execution-ready plan: route geometry, timing, altitude or airspace constraints, target or area coordinates, payload mode or pointing settings, and any command, rules-of-engagement, or coordination constraints. If one of those is missing, the plan should stay incomplete and clearly show what still needs to be provided. If inputs conflict, the system should flag the conflict and block execution until it is resolved or an authorized user overrides it.

topics.topic_content: Environmental, deployment, and platform constraints on the control system

slots.value: Deployments may be on different ground stations or command setups, with the controlling station able to change; authority must move cleanly with the aircraft to avoid ambiguity. The system should also distinguish local, remote, primary, and backup stations, and support setups where some stations only monitor while others can fully command, including coalition operations and reach-back support sites. A station may be monitor-only when it lacks current authority, when the link is too limited for safe command, or when policy restricts command because of mission sensitivity, certification, or airspace constraints. A station may command when it has assigned control authority, the communications path is good enough, and the operator is cleared for that mission segment. The role can change during the mission, especially during handoff between sites or if the primary station loses connectivity and a backup takes over.

slots.value: Phased migration rather than a big-bang cutover, with platforms moved over one at a time or by mission set; current missions and aircraft stay on legacy systems until the common system proves it can handle the same workflows with acceptable risk; operators can transition with minimal retraining and no interruption to active operations. A specialized, not-yet-integrated, or security-constrained UAV can remain on a separate workflow if moving it would interrupt a critical mission, expose an accreditation gap, or force the crew to use an unsupported workaround. It should move into the common control system only after required interfaces are validated, security and certification are approved, and operators can perform the mission end to end without losing any required capability. A platform is ready to migrate only when its core flight, payload, and mission-control functions are proven in the new system and the operators have a safe way to execute the normal mission set. If a mission is already in progress, cutover should not be forced mid-flight unless there is a very clear operational need and a validated handoff procedure; otherwise it should wait until the aircraft is back in a stable state. If the new system does not yet support a workflow with acceptable risk, that mission or platform should remain on the legacy system until the gap is closed or a constrained interim process is approved. Broad trigger conditions include demonstrated parity for essential functions, operator training readiness, and a verified fallback path if the new system fails. Anything still dependent on an unsupported payload, interface, or handoff behavior should not migrate. The exact cutover thresholds, sequencing by platform, and any waiver process remain tentative and open until integration results are seen.

topics.topic_content: Response times and accuracy expectations for mission operations

slots.value: Response urgency varies by mission phase and decision type: in launch, recovery, or any degraded state it needs to be essentially immediate because the aircraft may not tolerate delay; in steady-state cruise or routine sensing there is usually a little more time. If the aircraft is still controllable, the goal is to preserve options; once it is already in recovery, the window tightens and the fastest safe action or escalation should be prioritized.

revisions.new_value: Response should occur within the operational window where the aircraft is still safe and the mission can still be recovered; no fixed number provided yet.

revisions.old_value: Response should occur within the operational window where the aircraft is still safe and the mission can still be recovered; no fixed number provided yet.

slots.value: Accept some latency, but the acceptable amount depends on the platform and mission phase; no universal number should be set without checking. The system should make it obvious when the display is behind the feed, warn the operator or switch to a degraded indication if the delay crosses an operational threshold, and prevent time-sensitive decisions if the lag becomes severe enough to affect safety until it recovers. Decision behavior should be driven by mission phase, platform type, and the type of information displayed, with safety-critical phases using the strictest behavior: slight delay may merit only a delay label, materially stale data should switch to a degraded view, and lag that could mislead a time-sensitive action should block use for that purpose and force reliance on current status or another source. Thresholds should be configurable by program or mission profile. The main driver should be the mission’s safety and time sensitivity, not just the source or update rate by itself. If the information is slower but still operationally useful, a delayed label is fine; if it could mislead judgment, it should move to a degraded presentation; and if using it could create a safety risk in that phase, it should be blocked for time-sensitive use.

topics.topic_content: Mission continuity, resilience, and recovery expectations

slots.value: Must stay usable when links degrade so operators can still monitor status, queue actions, and recover a mission even if they can't do everything in real time; real-time essentials include basic aircraft status, link status, location, fuel or endurance, major faults, and payload state if it affects flight or safety, while detailed health trends, full sensor housekeeping, and non-urgent mission logs can be queued for later. The interface should adapt by phase and condition: during launch and recovery it should emphasize aircraft health, link quality, and immediate safety cues; en route it should lean toward route, fuel or endurance, and task progress; during target or collection activity it should put the payload view and mission objective front and center; in degraded operation it should shift hard toward fault status, lost-link handling, and quick recovery decision support.

slots.value: Needs very clean handoff between operators or control stations; must account for degraded communications, lost-link recovery, missions where payload tasking changes while the aircraft is already underway, different ground stations or command setups, varying sensor loads, differing automation levels, and transitions between local crew, remote crew, or control elements. The mission commander should be able to pause the mission, override a specific operator action, reassign tasks, take full control for safety, communications loss, or a major mission deviation, and hand control back to the operator once the situation is resolved and the transfer is acknowledged. Anything indicating imminent loss of vehicle, loss of control, or a critical subsystem failure should trigger an automatic safeguard or mission pause even if nobody can respond right away. The controlling station may change, and authority needs to move cleanly with the aircraft so there’s no ambiguity about who can command it. The system should support intermittent links, delayed updates, and a clear state showing whether a station is local, remote, primary, or backup. Allowed actions may differ by setup, since some ground stations might only monitor while others can fully command, especially during coalition operations or when a platform is being supported from a reach-back site. A station is monitor-only when it doesn’t have the current authority, when the link is too limited for safe command, or when policy restricts it because of mission sensitivity, certification, or airspace constraints. It can command when it has the assigned control authority, the communications path is good enough, and the operator is cleared for that mission segment. That role can change during the mission, especially during handoff between sites or if the primary station loses connectivity and a backup has to take over. When new tasking arrives while the aircraft is already underway, the current mission plan should be preserved rather than overwritten, the new tasking should be shown as a change or re-tasking request, and the operator should decide whether it can be merged, queued, or whether the aircraft must transition to a new profile. For preplanned surveillance, keep the approved route and payload setup unless an operator explicitly authorizes a change. For time-sensitive retasks, support quick acceptance, impact assessment, and a clear indication of what in the current plan is being displaced. In degraded communications or lost-link recovery, handling should be more protective, with automatic safing and only limited changes allowed until control is re-established; payload changes underway should be possible only if the platform and payload can verify the change safely without interrupting flight. The handoff should make the new station state very explicit with a visible indication of who currently has authority, who is in standby, and whether the aircraft is in transition. It should lock out simultaneous command from multiple stations and require a clean acknowledgment from both outgoing and incoming controllers so there is no overlap. If the handoff is incomplete or the link is unstable, the system should hold the aircraft in a safe interim state and keep command with the last confirmed authority until the transfer is resolved. The active mission should be shown as owned by the current controlling station or unit, while new tasking should be shown as a pending proposal or external request until approved and applied, and queued requests should remain visibly separate from the live mission state until authorized. If the request is just informational or still under review, it should stay separate from the live mission. If it’s compatible with the current route, payload, timing, and authority, then it can be linked or merged so the operator can apply it without rebuilding the mission from scratch. If it’s related but not yet approved, I’d want it shown alongside the live mission as a candidate change so the controller can compare them without any risk of accidentally executing it. If a retask fits within the current authority and doesn’t conflict with a critical phase of flight or collection, the system should accept it quickly and immediately assess what it would displace. It should then show the operator the impact on timing, route, payload use, and any already approved tasking before anything is executed. If the displacement is significant or could create a safety or mission conflict, it should hold for review rather than auto-applying. It should require an explicit acknowledgment from the command-and-control side, not just receipt of the message. At minimum, the system should see that the tasking was accepted and validated by the external side before it marks the handoff complete and activates the new mission details. If that acknowledgment does not come back, the handoff should stay pending and the operator should be alerted. It should show a clear pending-handoff status with the reason, the elapsed wait time, and what mission elements are still not authoritative. After a defined timeout, it should escalate to the operator and perhaps a supervisor or alternate channel, but it should not auto-complete the tasking unless that is explicitly approved by policy. If the mission has to continue, the system should keep the previous confirmed tasking active until the new acknowledgment arrives or an authorized contingency is invoked.

slots.value: Phased migration rather than a big-bang cutover, bringing platforms over one at a time or by mission set; broad trigger conditions should include demonstrated parity for essential functions, operator training readiness, and a verified fallback path if the new system fails, while anything still dependent on an unsupported payload, interface, or handoff behavior should not migrate yet. Exact cutover thresholds, sequencing by platform, and any waiver process remain tentative until integration results are seen.

slots.value: Current missions and aircraft need to keep running on the legacy systems until the common system proves it can handle the same workflows with acceptable risk. Exceptions may remain on separate workflows for a while if a platform is highly specialized, not yet integrated, or tied to a mission with unique security or operational constraints. The decision rule is mission risk and readiness, not convenience: a UAV can stay separate if moving it would interrupt a critical mission, expose an accreditation gap, force the crew to use an unsupported workaround, or cause loss of an approved mission capability during transition. If the new system does not yet support a workflow with acceptable risk, then that mission or platform should remain on the legacy system until the gap is closed or a constrained interim process is approved.

slots.key: Response urgency by mission phase and controllability
slots.value: Urgency changes by platform and mission phase, and the rule should also depend on the type of information being displayed. Safety-critical phases use the strictest behavior. If the data is only slightly behind, a delay label may be enough; if it is materially stale, the system should switch to a degraded view; and if the lag could mislead a time-sensitive action, it should block use for that purpose and force the operator to rely on current status or a different source. These thresholds should be configurable by program or mission profile because what is acceptable on one vehicle or phase may be unacceptable on another.

revisions.new_value: Urgency changes a lot by mission phase and by what decision is being made. In launch, recovery, or any degraded state, the response needs to be essentially immediate because the aircraft may not tolerate delay; during steady-state cruise or routine sensing, there is usually a little more time. If the aircraft is still controllable, options should be preserved; once it is already in recovery, the window tightens and the system should prioritize the fastest safe action or escalation.

slots.key: Authority and approval requirements for mission changes
slots.value: For approved preplanned surveillance, any change that affects where the aircraft goes, what the sensor is looking at, when it collects, or how it behaves requires explicit operator authorization before execution. topics.topic_content: Protection of operational information, access, and mission products

slots.value: Common role should hide platform variation as much as possible; only platform-supported mission types, control modes, and sensor commands should be shown; unsupported actions must be blocked; certain platform-specific functions may require additional clearance or tighter control depending on mission and aircraft configuration. Tighter controls should apply to anything that can directly affect safety, legality, or mission sensitivity, including arming or disarming payloads, changing flight envelope limits, altering navigation routes in restricted airspace, and using specialized sensors or weapons where those exist. Limits are triggered by mission phase, aircraft type, airspace restrictions, classification or handling rules for the data, degraded conditions that make the aircraft less predictable, and especially critical phases like launch, recovery, or contested airspace. The controlling station may change, and authority must move cleanly with the aircraft so there is no ambiguity about who can command it; allowed actions may also differ by setup, with some ground stations only monitoring while others can fully command. A station is monitor-only when it doesn’t have current authority, when the link is too limited for safe command, or when policy restricts it because of mission sensitivity, certification, or airspace constraints. It can command when it has assigned control authority, the communications path is good enough, and the operator is cleared for that mission segment. Role can change during the mission, especially during handoff between sites or if the primary station loses connectivity and a backup takes over.

slots.key: Classification handling and data release controls
slots.value: Access should be based on role, mission need, and classification or releasability rules, so not everyone who can see a mission can necessarily see every target or product. Raw sensor data should be protected more tightly than processed products, because raw data may expose sources, methods, or details not meant for broad distribution. The system should support controlled release, auditing, and metadata marking so that when products are handed off, only the approved content and context go with them. Forwarding and repackaging should be limited to users or systems with the right role and release authority, and each handoff should preserve the original markings and any handling caveats. In many cases, a processed product should be shared instead of the raw data if that meets the tasking need, to protect sensitive collection details while still giving commanders the information they need.

sections.section_content: Deployment, Transition, Maintenance, and Requirement Prioritization

topics.topic_content: Introduction of the common control system across current and future UAV programs

slots.key: Migration path from existing control systems
slots.value: Phased migration rather than a big-bang cutover; current missions and aircraft keep running on legacy systems until the common system proves it can handle the same workflows with acceptable risk; platforms move over one at a time or by mission set; operators transition with minimal retraining and no interruption to active operations. A platform is ready to migrate only when its core flight, payload, and mission-control functions are proven in the new system and operators have a safe way to execute the normal mission set. If a mission is already in progress, cutover should not be forced mid-flight unless there is a very clear operational need and a validated handoff procedure; otherwise it should wait until the aircraft is back in a stable state. If the new system does not yet support a workflow with acceptable risk, the mission or platform should remain on the legacy system until the gap is closed or a constrained interim process is approved. Broad trigger conditions include demonstrated parity for essential functions, operator training readiness, and a verified fallback path if the new system fails. Anything still dependent on an unsupported payload, interface, or handoff behavior should not migrate yet. Exact cutover thresholds, sequencing by platform, and any waiver process remain tentative until integration results are seen.

slots.key: Business rationale for common UAV control system
slots.value: Reduce the number of separate tools and training pipelines to maintain across programs; lower integration cost; make operator transition between platforms easier; create a path to bring future UAVs into the same control environment without starting over each time. Exceptions may exist for a while when a platform is highly specialized, not yet integrated, or tied to a mission with unique security or operational constraints. At the enterprise level, reducing tool sprawl and training burden is a firm direction, while the exact scope of which workflows must stay common and which can diverge by program remains tentative until user groups and platform specifics are confirmed.

slots.value: A person switching between mission roles must either have a system-confirmed handoff or an approved role change before acting in a new role, so they are not operating in two conflicting roles at once without the system knowing. Role precedence should follow the current mission phase and the role with the highest immediate safety or operational impact; for example, in a critical control phase, aircraft control takes priority over planning or distribution, and payload operation does not supersede it unless it is explicitly assigned and safe to do so. When phases overlap or change suddenly, the most immediate safety-of-flight or mission-survival need governs priority, with aircraft control and recovery-type actions automatically elevated ahead of planning, payload work, or product distribution whenever there is conflict; the current task is suspended or downgraded until the higher-priority control need is satisfied, unless an authorized exception is specifically declared.

revisions.new_value: A supervisor or mission commander can step in when there is a safety issue, an unexpected change in the mission, a communications problem, or anything that pushes the aircraft outside the planned envelope. In that situation they may approve a high-risk action, override a planned task, or take control if the operator cannot continue safely or the mission needs to be redirected quickly. Their authority is to protect the mission and the aircraft and keep the operation aligned with command intent.

slots.key: Degraded communications and lost-link recovery handling
slots.value: Use protective handling with automatic safing and only limited changes allowed until control is re-established; unique lost-link behavior may still require a program-specific control rule or restriction. During degraded communications, the operator should be able to command a safe fallback, redirect the aircraft if link still permits, or approve recovery actions, while the system automatically handles the low-level stability and timeout behavior. If the link is fully lost, the system should follow preapproved lost-link logic without waiting for operator input.

slots.value: Exact timing thresholds and platform-specific edge cases, including that operators may only command route, payload state, or recovery behavior changes once the aircraft is in a stable state for that transition; sequencing must be enforced for the specific platform; route changes must not interrupt launch, recovery, or a critical payload action; payload state changes must be blocked outside approved conditions; recovery-behavior changes are especially sensitive and may only be allowed when the aircraft is in a state where the new behavior can take over safely. Thresholds for delayed display handling are configurable by program or mission profile, and what is acceptable depends on mission phase, platform type, and the type of information being displayed.

slots.key: UI layout emphasis by mission phase and degraded condition
slots.value: The interface should adapt by phase and condition: during launch and recovery it should emphasize aircraft health, link quality, and immediate safety cues; en route it should lean toward route, fuel or endurance, and task progress; during target or collection activity it should put the payload view and mission objective front and center; in degraded operation it should shift hard toward fault status, lost-link handling, and quick recovery decision support.

slots.value: If data is only slightly behind, label it as delayed; if it is materially stale, switch to a degraded view; if the lag could mislead a time-sensitive action, block use for that purpose and force the operator to rely on current status or a different source. The main driver should be the mission’s safety and time sensitivity, not just the source or update rate by itself. The system should also consider the source’s declared freshness and confidence, because different sensors and external feeds won’t age the same way. Trusted onboard sensors can probably stay usable a little longer if the feed is continuous and the health checks are good, while external feeds should be treated more conservatively because their timing and provenance can be less certain. The system should combine declared freshness, confidence, and source trust into a single status so that low-confidence or stale external information drops to degraded or blocked sooner for time-sensitive decisions.

topics.topic_content: Priorities, acceptance expectations, and unresolved delivery risks

slots.value: Provide operators one consistent way to plan, task, and control missions across UAV platforms, supporting reliable mission planning, real-time control and monitoring, payload and sensor handling, imagery/mission product distribution, and continuous aircraft status visibility, with a path for future UAVs to enter the same control environment without starting over.

slots.key: Acceptance criteria for mission control and product dissemination
slots.value: Must support both routine and dynamic operations, including preplanned surveillance missions handled differently from time-sensitive retasks against new targets, with very clean handoff between operators or control stations; also needs to account for degraded communications, lost-link recovery, and missions where payload tasking changes while the aircraft is already underway.

revisions.new_value: Must support both routine and dynamic operations, allowing operators to react to changing tasking, update missions quickly, pass information back into the broader command-and-control environment, and maintain interoperability/common workflow across current and future aircraft without separate platform handling.

slots.value: Exceptions may be needed for a while; specialized, not-yet-integrated platforms or missions with unique security/operational constraints may remain on separate workflows until safely absorbed. Key constraints include mission criticality, integration effort, certification/accreditation issues, and whether the common system can support required payload or control functions without workaround.
